title: Depth In The Management Chain
description:
Every employee sits somewhere in a management tree. Report each employee's depth, where an employee with no manager is at depth 1, their direct reports at depth 2, and so on.

Name the columns `name` and `depth`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
WITH RECURSIVE chain(id, name, depth) AS (
  SELECT id, name, 1 FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, c.depth + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT name, depth FROM chain;
hint: A recursive CTE: the anchor picks the roots (no manager), the recursive arm joins children to already-found parents and adds one.
outputExplanation: Top-level (manager_id IS NULL): Ava, Eve, Hal → depth 1. Their direct reports: Ben, Cara, Dan report to Ava; Finn, Gia report to Eve → depth 2. The recursive CTE's anchor picks the roots, and each recursive step adds one to the depth.

title: Total Team Size Including Indirect Reports
description:
For every employee who manages at least one person, report how many people sit below them in the tree — direct reports plus everyone under those reports, all the way down.

Name the columns `manager` and `team_size`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
WITH RECURSIVE tree(root, id) AS (
  SELECT manager_id, id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT t.root, e.id
  FROM employees e
  JOIN tree t ON e.manager_id = t.id
)
SELECT m.name AS manager, COUNT(*) AS team_size
FROM tree t
JOIN employees m ON m.id = t.root
GROUP BY t.root, m.name;
hint: Seed the recursion with every (manager, direct report) pair, then keep attaching each report's own reports to the same root.
outputExplanation: Ava has 3 total people below her in the tree (Ben, Cara, Dan — all direct). Eve has 2 (Finn, Gia — all direct). Hal manages nobody → excluded by `WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL`. The recursive CTE starts from each (manager, direct report) pair and traverses all descendants, grouping by the original root manager.

title: Above Your Department's Median
description:
Report every employee whose salary is strictly above the **median** salary of their own department. Ignore employees with a NULL salary.

Name the columns `dept_id`, `name` and `salary`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT dept_id, name, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS cnt
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
),
medians AS (
  SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS med
  FROM ranked
  WHERE rn IN ((cnt + 1) / 2, (cnt + 2) / 2)
  GROUP BY dept_id
)
SELECT r.dept_id, r.name, r.salary
FROM ranked r
JOIN medians m ON m.dept_id = r.dept_id
WHERE r.salary > m.med;
hint: Number the rows inside each department, then average the one or two middle positions — (cnt+1)/2 and (cnt+2)/2 land on the same row when the count is odd.
outputExplanation: Engineering salaries (non-NULL): 95k, 120k, 120k, 150k → median = (120k + 120k) / 2 = 120k → Ava(150k) > 120k qualifies. Sales salaries: 70k, 85k, 130k → median = 85k → Eve(130k) > 85k qualifies. HR has only 1 salary → median = Hal's own 60k, nobody can exceed it.

title: Cumulative Share Of Payroll
description:
Order employees by salary from highest to lowest (ties broken by `id`) and report the running percentage of total company payroll accounted for by everyone down to and including that employee, rounded to 2 decimals.

Name the columns `name`, `salary` and `running_pct`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT name, salary,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, id
                                       ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
             / SUM(salary) OVER (), 2) AS running_pct
FROM employees;
hint: Two windows in one SELECT: a running SUM with a frame, divided by a grand-total SUM OVER () with no partition.
outputExplanation: Ordered by salary descending: Ava(150k)→18.07% of total (150k/830k), Eve(130k)→33.73% (cumulative 280k/830k), Ben(120k)→48.19%, Cara(120k)→62.65%, Dan(95k)→74.10%, Gia(85k)→84.34%, Finn(70k)→92.77%, Hal(60k)→100%. The running sum divided by the grand total gives the cumulative share.

title: Second Highest Salary Per Department
description:
For each department report the second highest **distinct** salary and everyone earning it. Departments without a second distinct salary produce no rows.

Name the columns `dept_id`, `name` and `salary`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT dept_id, name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
WHERE rnk = 2;
hint: DENSE_RANK numbers distinct salaries, so rank 2 is exactly the second distinct value — and it disappears on its own when there isn't one.
outputExplanation: Engineering distinct salaries: 150k (rank 1), 120k (rank 2), 95k (rank 3) → rank 2 = Ben and Cara at $120k. Sales distinct salaries: 130k (rank 1), 85k (rank 2), 70k (rank 3) → rank 2 = Gia at $85k. HR has only one distinct salary → no rank 2, zero rows for HR. DENSE_RANK by salary, filtered to rnk = 2.

title: Print The Reporting Line
description:
For every employee report their full reporting line from the top of the company down to them, as a single string joined by ` > `. For example an engineer under a manager under a CEO reads `CEO > Manager > Engineer` (using their names).

Name the columns `name` and `chain`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
WITH RECURSIVE line(id, name, chain) AS (
  SELECT id, name, name FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, l.chain || ' > ' || e.name
  FROM employees e
  JOIN line l ON e.manager_id = l.id
)
SELECT name, chain FROM line;
hint: Carry the accumulated string down the recursion, appending with the || operator.
outputExplanation: Top-level: Ava → "Ava", Eve → "Eve", Hal → "Hal". Ben → "Ava > Ben", Cara → "Ava > Cara", Dan → "Ava > Dan". Finn → "Eve > Finn", Gia → "Eve > Gia". The recursive CTE builds the chain by appending each child's name to the parent's chain with `|| ' > ' ||` concatenation.

title: Departments Where Everybody Clears 70k
description:
Report the name of every department in which **every** employee earns more than 70000. A department with no employees does not qualify, and an employee with a NULL salary disqualifies their department.

Name the column `department`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT d.name AS department
FROM departments d
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.id)
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM employees e
    WHERE e.dept_id = d.id
      AND (e.salary IS NULL OR e.salary <= 70000)
  );
hint: "All rows satisfy X" is easiest as "no row violates X" — but you still need an EXISTS to rule out empty departments.

title: Salary Percentile Rank
description:
For every employee with a salary, report their percentile rank in the company — the fraction of employees earning strictly less than them, as a percentage rounded to 2 decimals.

Name the columns `name` and `percentile`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT name,
       ROUND(100.0 * (COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY salary RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
                      - COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY salary))
             / COUNT(*) OVER (), 2) AS percentile
FROM employees
WHERE salary IS NOT NULL;
hint: A RANGE frame counts every row with an equal salary, so subtract the size of the tie group to get "strictly less than".
outputExplanation: Hal(60k): 0 of 8 employees strictly below him → 0%. Finn(70k): 1 below → 12.5%. Gia(85k): 2 below → 25%. Dan(95k): 3 below → 37.5%. Ben/Cara(120k, tied): 4 below each → 50%. Eve(130k): 6 below → 75%. Ava(150k): 7 below → 87.5%. The `RANGE` frame counts rows with equal salaries as a peer group, which is subtracted to get the "strictly less than" count.

title: Hired In The Same Month
description:
Report every pair of different employees hired in the same calendar month of the same year. List each pair once, with the lower `id` first.

Name the columns `first_name`, `second_name` and `month`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT a.name AS first_name, b.name AS second_name,
       strftime('%Y-%m', a.hire_date) AS month
FROM employees a
JOIN employees b
  ON a.id < b.id
 AND strftime('%Y-%m', a.hire_date) = strftime('%Y-%m', b.hire_date);
hint: Joining on a.id < b.id (rather than <>) is what stops each pair appearing twice.
outputExplanation: Only Ben and Cara were hired in the same calendar month of the same year — both on 2019-03 → one pair (Ben, Cara). The self-join condition `a.id < b.id` ensures each pair appears only once, not twice.

title: Pay Compression Ratio
description:
For each department that has at least two employees with a salary, report the ratio of its highest salary to its lowest, rounded to 2 decimals. Skip departments whose lowest salary is 0 or negative, since the ratio is meaningless there.

Name the columns `department` and `ratio`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT d.name AS department,
       ROUND(1.0 * MAX(e.salary) / MIN(e.salary), 2) AS ratio
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 AND MIN(e.salary) > 0;
hint: Everything you need is in HAVING: both the count check and the guard against a zero or negative denominator.
outputExplanation: Engineering: max 150k / min 95k = 1.58. Sales: max 130k / min 70k = 1.86. HR excluded: only 1 employee with salary → `HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2` fails. The `MIN > 0` guard in HAVING also prevents division by zero or negative ratios.
